title: Diversify with participation

blocks.heading: Diversify with participation
blocks.text: Tourism can diversify rural livelihoods beyond a narrow productive base, while remaining dependent on demand and suitable access. Local ownership, employment or supply links are needed for retained benefits. Diversification does not remove seasonality, environmental costs or the need for other livelihoods.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Cultural tourism
blocks.text: Cultural tourism involves visitors’ interest in cultural knowledge, practices, heritage or activities. Community control and consent can support income and valued heritage; pressure to perform, unequal returns or intrusion can harm participants. Judge benefits under terms people can influence.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Conservation and participation
blocks.text: Community participation can connect conservation decisions with local knowledge, rights and benefits. Conservation-related visitor income can support habitat protection where local owners, workers or suppliers retain benefits; restricted access or unequal returns can weaken support.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Evaluate retained gains
blocks.text: A fictional guesthouse can buy meals from a village group or import prepared meals. Local purchasing may retain income and support skills, but the group must meet agreed food standards and delivery times. Imported meals may be easier to arrange initially while offering fewer local supplier links. Compare feasibility, working conditions and retained spending; visitor numbers alone do not measure community benefit.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Conservancies as a Namibian example
blocks.text: Namibian communal conservancies illustrate community involvement in wildlife management and associated tourism opportunities. Local guides, accommodation work and supply contracts can retain income and support incentives to protect wildlife. Community decision rules and the distribution of returns matter: wildlife damage, restricted access and unequal benefits can impose costs. A conservancy is therefore an example to evaluate, rather than automatic proof that conservation has improved all livelihoods. Compare retained earnings, community influence, habitat condition and residents’ costs using evidence for the particular place and period.
